subject: Distribution of predictor variables in DSM and selecting non-significant variables

messages.author: 3078d91cce33ad91
messages.subject: Distribution of predictor variables in DSM and selecting non-significant variables
parts:
Hi Everyone,


Sorry for more questions so soon.


1. Should explanatory variables for the DSM/GAM be normally distributed (or close to normal), or rather their residuals, even if this requires transformation? I understand that the response variable in a GAM does not need to be normally distributed but I have not been able to find much information, nor a consistent answer, anywhere regarding the predictor variables.


2. Can you provide any advice on selecting predictor variables to keep in the DSM when none are showing up as significant according to p-values in the DSM/GAM but a reasonable amount of deviance is being explained by the model e.g. 40+%? I am planning on trying different segment sizes in the DSM to see if this makes a difference but I am also curious if the distribution of predictor variables will have an effect (hence my question above) and I am also considering trying Principal Components in the DSM to see if this improves predictor significance and model performance.


Any guidance you can provide is appreciated.


Many thanks,

Luke.

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distribution of predictor variables in DSM and selecting non-significant variables
parts:
Hi Luke, hi listfolk,

1. There are no distributional assumptions on the explanatory variables.

2. This is tricky. I don't recommend using PCA or some other
variable-globbing scheme, as you'll lose any interpretability in the
model. Have you tried just using smooths of location (projected)? This
is a kind of catch-all in the model (since all your other environmental
variables will vary in space anyway), so might get you somewhere. You
might also want to investigate including your covariates as linear terms
in the model and see whether there is much benefit to including
smoothers at all(!). Another option would be to switch basis to a
"shrinkage" approach (bs="ts" or bs="cs" in each s() term) as these will
totally remove non-useful terms in the model and you can see what's left
(normally the linear bits are left in).

Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave

messages.author: 3078d91cce33ad91
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distribution of predictor variables in DSM and selecting non-significant variables
parts:
Hi Dave,

Thank you again for the really useful advice! I will continue trying the things you suggest. 

I actually ran another model using the same covariates but with a segment size of 200m long rather than 100m and the deviance explained went from 40% to 60% but still none of the variables were significant! When I run the model with bs='ts' and/or select = TRUE, the deviance explained drops to 26% and still no variables are significant. Hence I wonder if it is possible that numerous environmental variables each contribute a little to the observed variation in animal density without any single variable contributing enough to be considered significant...? Is this something you have experienced before? 

I will keep playing around with different variables and the various modelling options you suggested and see what I find. I'm sure I'll report back some results, as no doubt I will be asking for some more advice!

Many thanks,
Luke.
